beats.narration_text: Bonjour. This is Liam, in for Bear. Say you have a thousand questions for Claude. You could send them one at a time and wait on each. But if the answers can wait, you can send them all as one batch, at half the price. So the real question is how to hand Claude the whole pile at once.

beats.narration_text: A batch: a list of requests you send together and collect later. A custom ID: the tag you put on each request. And a result: what comes back for each one, saying whether it succeeded or errored.

beats.narration_text: The usual way is a loop. Send one request, wait for its answer, then send the next. A thousand questions means a thousand waits, and every one is billed at the standard price.

beats.narration_text: A batch is the same requests, in one list. Each one is an ordinary Messages request, plus a custom ID: a tag you choose, like question zero, question one. That tag is how you find its answer later.

beats.narration_text: Then it runs asynchronously. Each request is handled on its own, so one failing doesn't hold up the rest. The docs say most batches finish within an hour, and a batch that isn't done within twenty four hours expires.

shot.visual_intent: The Claude box sits at the left ('Claude'); four lanes run from it to the right; the sealed envelopes ride along them at different speeds and a lamp at the end of each lane lights terracotta as it arrives, in the order 2, 0, 3, 1; then 'most: under 1 hour' and '24 h limit' land at the top.

beats.narration_text: Meanwhile, your code polls. Every so often it asks for the batch's status. It says in progress until every request has finished. Then it flips to ended, and the results are ready.

beats.narration_text: The results come back as one list, but in any order. The docs say so plainly. So never match by position. Match by custom ID. The answer tagged two goes with the request tagged two.

shot.visual_intent: The four sealed envelopes in a row at the top ('requests'); four kraft answer cards slide out of the Claude box into a row below in the order 2, 0, 3, 1 ('results'); then each answer card moves under the envelope with the same tag ('by custom_id').

beats.narration_text: Each result also says how it went. Most say succeeded, with Claude's message inside. One might say errored, and errored requests aren't billed. So you send just the failed ones again.

shot.visual_intent: The matched pairs: ink checks land beside answers 0, 2 and 3 ('succeeded'); an ink cross lands beside answer 1 ('errored'); answer 1 clears, and envelope 1 rides back into the Claude box on its own.

beats.narration_text: And the payoff. Anthropic's docs say all batch usage is charged at fifty percent of standard API prices. The trade is time, and results stay available for twenty nine days. If the answers can wait, they cost half.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude Code, in a repo with a script that calls Claude in a loop: Find the loop in this repo that calls the Claude API once per item. Rewrite it as a Message Batches job: give each request a valid custom ID built from the item's key, submit them as one batch, poll until processing status is ended, then match each result to its item by custom ID and print any that errored. Then check two things yourself. Does every item get exactly one result, matched by its custom ID? And are the errored ones printed, not silently dropped?
